16641.sourceSearchName: clus lib attribute value variant clus lib attribute value variant
16641.title: ClusLib Attribute Value Variant
16641.heading: ClusLib Attribute Value Variant
16641.content:
AttrValue stores an individual attribute as a Boost variant capable of holding the supported underlying value forms. The value object does not decide how a categorical code or continuous number should be interpreted; that responsibility belongs to attribute metadata.

A variant is more type-safe than an untagged union because retrieval checks the active type. Separating storage from interpretation lets records use one vector type across numeric, categorical, identifier, and label fields.

16642.sourceSearchName: clus lib attribute value variant clus lib attribute value variant
16642.title: ClusLib Attribute Value Variant
16642.heading: References

16643.sourceSearchName: clus lib attribute information base clus lib attribute information base
16643.title: ClusLib Attribute Information Base
16643.heading: Document

16644.sourceSearchName: clus lib attribute information base clus lib attribute information base
16644.title: ClusLib Attribute Information Base
16644.heading: ClusLib Attribute Information Base
16644.content:
AttrInfo is the polymorphic metadata base for an attribute. It records common identity and type behavior and defines virtual operations for setting, retrieving, comparing, and measuring values through the corresponding AttrValue objects.

Continuous and discrete subclasses implement type-specific semantics behind that interface. Algorithms can traverse a schema uniformly while runtime dispatch selects the correct handling for each component.

16645.sourceSearchName: clus lib attribute information base clus lib attribute information base
16645.title: ClusLib Attribute Information Base
16645.heading: References

16646.sourceSearchName: clus lib algorithm base class clus lib algorithm base class
16646.title: ClusLib Algorithm Base Class
16646.heading: Document

16647.sourceSearchName: clus lib algorithm base class clus lib algorithm base class
16647.title: ClusLib Algorithm Base Class
16647.heading: ClusLib Algorithm Base Class
16647.content:
Algorithm is the polymorphic base for clustering methods. It owns Arguments and mutable Results, retains the dataset used during computation, exposes configuration and result access, and defines the public clusterize operation.

A virtual destructor and virtual lifecycle methods allow concrete algorithms to specialize behavior safely. The base class centralizes the contract that every method accepts inputs, performs clustering, and publishes results.

16648.sourceSearchName: clus lib algorithm base class clus lib algorithm base class
16648.title: ClusLib Algorithm Base Class

16649.sourceSearchName: cloud based collaboration cloud based collaboration
16649.title: Cloud-Based Collaboration
16649.heading: Document

16650.sourceSearchName: cloud based collaboration cloud based collaboration
16650.title: Cloud-Based Collaboration
16650.heading: Cloud-Based Collaboration
16650.content:
Cloud-based collaboration provides shared documents, messaging, email, conferencing, and other group communication through network-hosted services. It shifts the center of collaboration from software installed on one operating system to services reachable across devices and locations.

The model supports distributed work but makes provider dependency and shared information security central concerns. Independent backups and open file formats can reduce the cost of losing or changing the collaboration provider.

16651.sourceSearchName: cloud based collaboration cloud based collaboration
16651.title: Cloud-Based Collaboration
16651.heading: References

16652.sourceSearchName: cloud enabled business scalability cloud enabled business scalability
16652.title: Cloud-Enabled Business Scalability
16652.heading: Document

16653.sourceSearchName: cloud enabled business scalability cloud enabled business scalability
16653.title: Cloud-Enabled Business Scalability
16653.heading: Cloud-Enabled Business Scalability
16653.content:
Cloud-enabled business scalability is the ability to expand a product, service, or organization rapidly by obtaining computing, information, and automated processes without building every supporting system first. Network delivery also gives a small organization access to geographically broad markets.

Technical capacity is only one constraint. Business processes, support, security, supplier relationships, and revenue must scale with demand or the cloud merely moves the bottleneck elsewhere.

16654.sourceSearchName: cloud enabled business scalability cloud enabled business scalability
16654.title: Cloud-Enabled Business Scalability
16654.heading: References

16655.sourceSearchName: cloud based office productivity cloud based office productivity
16655.title: Cloud-Based Office Productivity
16655.heading: Document

16656.sourceSearchName: cloud based office productivity cloud based office productivity
16656.title: Cloud-Based Office Productivity
16656.heading: Cloud-Based Office Productivity
16656.content:
Cloud-based office productivity delivers word processing, spreadsheets, presentations, and related tools as hosted applications. Users can work from different devices, store documents remotely, and collaborate on shared content without distributing the full software stack to every workstation.

Central updates and reduced endpoint management can lower operating effort. Data protection, open export formats, backup independence, provider availability, and total ownership cost remain important because everyday business work depends on the service.

16657.sourceSearchName: cloud based office productivity cloud based office productivity
16657.title: Cloud-Based Office Productivity
16657.heading: References

16658.sourceSearchName: cloud web hosting cloud web hosting
16658.title: Cloud Web Hosting
16658.heading: Document
16658.content:
2026-09-08 22:39

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Cloud Service and Deployment Models]]

16659.sourceSearchName: cloud web hosting cloud web hosting
16659.title: Cloud Web Hosting
16659.heading: Cloud Web Hosting
16659.content:
Cloud web hosting runs a website on infrastructure or a platform that can change capacity with demand. Web traffic often varies by hour, day, campaign, or product launch, so a fixed environment may alternate between idle excess and inadequate peak capacity.

[[Rapid Elasticity]] and consumption-oriented pricing fit this pattern because resources can scale out during a burst and scale in afterward. Application design, network capacity, measurements, and load tests are still needed to make that elasticity effective.

16660.sourceSearchName: cloud web hosting cloud web hosting
16660.title: Cloud Web Hosting
16660.heading: References

16661.sourceSearchName: cloud vendor evaluation cloud vendor evaluation
16661.title: Cloud Vendor Evaluation
16661.heading: Document

16662.sourceSearchName: cloud vendor evaluation cloud vendor evaluation
16662.title: Cloud Vendor Evaluation
16662.heading: Cloud Vendor Evaluation
16662.content:
Cloud vendor evaluation compares providers against the consumer's defined functional, nonfunctional, and business requirements. It examines service maturity, features, interoperability, security, resilience, capacity, price, support, continuity, and the transparency of reports and service levels.

The comparison should include the consequences of leaving as well as the experience of joining. A provider that scores well on current features may still be unsuitable if data cannot be exported or an equivalent service cannot take over.

16663.sourceSearchName: cloud vendor evaluation cloud vendor evaluation
16663.title: Cloud Vendor Evaluation
16663.heading: References

16664.sourceSearchName: cloud tax planning service cloud tax planning service
16664.title: Cloud Tax Planning Service
16664.heading: Document

16665.sourceSearchName: cloud tax planning service cloud tax planning service
16665.title: Cloud Tax Planning Service
16665.heading: Cloud Tax Planning Service
16665.content:
A cloud tax planning service composes current tax information, personal or business data, calculation applications, scenario comparison, and reporting into a coordinated process. Information retrieval should be automated so the workflow uses the applicable rules available at the time.

Human judgment can remain in the process when choosing among future scenarios. The service illustrates how [[Information as a Service]] and [[Software as a Service]] can become building blocks for [[Business Process as a Service]].

16666.sourceSearchName: cloud tax planning service cloud tax planning service
16666.title: Cloud Tax Planning Service
16666.heading: References

16667.sourceSearchName: cloud training service cloud training service
16667.title: Cloud Training Service
16667.heading: Document

16668.sourceSearchName: cloud training service cloud training service
16668.title: Cloud Training Service
16668.heading: Cloud Training Service
16668.content:
A cloud training service treats enrollment, content delivery, exercises, assessment, progress, and certification as a scalable process rather than only placing lecture material online. It can serve learners beyond the physical capacity and location of one institution.

Integrating identity and testing makes training closer to a complete business-process service. Customer-centered delivery should adapt the timing and path to the learner while preserving credible evidence of participation and achievement.

16669.sourceSearchName: cloud training service cloud training service
16669.title: Cloud Training Service
16669.heading: References

16670.sourceSearchName: cloud service requirements cloud service requirements
16670.title: Cloud Service Requirements
16670.heading: Document

16671.sourceSearchName: cloud service requirements cloud service requirements
16671.title: Cloud Service Requirements
16671.heading: Cloud Service Requirements
16671.content:
Cloud service requirements state the capabilities and constraints against which a service and provider will be evaluated. Functional requirements include maturity, features, interoperability, and the usage model; nonfunctional requirements include security, availability, resilience, and network capacity.

Business requirements cover pricing and value, risk, continuity, support, reporting, and billing. Turning these needs into measurable commitments prevents a technology label from substituting for evidence that the service fits its intended purpose.

16672.sourceSearchName: cloud service requirements cloud service requirements
16672.title: Cloud Service Requirements
16672.heading: References

16673.sourceSearchName: cloud storage service cloud storage service
16673.title: Cloud Storage Service
16673.heading: Document
16673.content:
2026-09-08 22:39

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Cloud Service and Deployment Models]]

16674.sourceSearchName: cloud storage service cloud storage service
16674.title: Cloud Storage Service
16674.heading: Cloud Storage Service
16674.content:
A cloud storage service supplies durable storage over a network as an infrastructure capability. It can hold media, documents, correspondence, backups, and application data while letting authorized users or applications reach them from multiple places and devices.

Providers can operate redundant disks and monitoring at a scale that is difficult for a small consumer to reproduce. The consumer must still plan encryption, access control, backup independence, restoration, retention, and the consequences of losing the provider.

16675.sourceSearchName: cloud storage service cloud storage service
16675.title: Cloud Storage Service
16675.heading: References

16677.title: Cloud Service
16677.heading: Cloud Service
16677.content:
A cloud service is a coordinated set of systems, components, and resources that implements a useful function or process for a consumer over a network. The consumer primarily evaluates the value delivered rather than the internal machines or software used to produce it.

Its expected scope, quality, and timeliness can be expressed in a [[Service Level Agreement]], while measurable internal targets are expressed as [[Service Level Objective]]s. A service must also exhibit the defining properties of [[Cloud Computing]] rather than merely being remotely hosted.

16679.sourceSearchName: cloud service pattern cloud service pattern
16679.title: Cloud Service Pattern
16679.heading: Document
16679.content:
2026-09-08 22:39

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Cloud Service Composition and Brokerage]]

16680.sourceSearchName: cloud service pattern cloud service pattern
16680.title: Cloud Service Pattern
16680.heading: Cloud Service Pattern
16680.content:
A cloud service pattern is a reusable description of how cloud capabilities solve a recurring use case. It gives the pattern a name, states the problem and circumstances, identifies component [[Cloud Cell]]s and their relationships, and records the tradeoffs or consequences.

A web-service pattern might combine web, database, storage, service-bus, and firewall cells with stated internal and external interfaces. The pattern supports repeatable architecture without requiring every implementation to be identical.

16681.sourceSearchName: cloud service pattern cloud service pattern
16681.title: Cloud Service Pattern
16681.heading: References

16682.sourceSearchName: cloud service model cloud service model
16682.title: Cloud Service Model
16682.heading: Document
16682.content:
2026-09-08 22:39

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Cloud Service and Deployment Models]]

16683.sourceSearchName: cloud service model cloud service model
16683.title: Cloud Service Model
16683.heading: Cloud Service Model
16683.content:
A cloud service model describes the level of abstraction at which a provider delivers computing capability. As the abstraction rises, the consumer manages fewer implementation details and receives a more complete function.

The principal levels discussed in the book are [[Infrastructure as a Service]], [[Platform as a Service]], [[Software as a Service]], [[Information as a Service]], and [[Business Process as a Service]]. A higher level can be built from services at the levels beneath it.

16684.sourceSearchName: cloud service model cloud service model
16684.title: Cloud Service Model
16684.heading: References

16685.sourceSearchName: cloud service provider cloud service provider
16685.title: Cloud Service Provider
16685.heading: Document
16685.content:
2026-09-08 22:39

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Cloud Service Composition and Brokerage]]

16686.sourceSearchName: cloud service provider cloud service provider
16686.title: Cloud Service Provider
16686.heading: Cloud Service Provider
16686.content:
A cloud service provider supplies a cloud service to consumers and orchestrates the resources required to activate it. The provider maintains the service offering, measures its operation, and agrees on a price and service commitment with the consumer.

The provider distinguishes cost from price: cost is what it bears to create and operate the service, while price is what it charges. A provider may build its own services as a [[Cloud Service Creator]] or combine services obtained elsewhere.

16687.sourceSearchName: cloud service provider cloud service provider
16687.title: Cloud Service Provider
16687.heading: References

16688.sourceSearchName: cloud service interoperability cloud service interoperability
16688.title: Cloud Service Interoperability
16688.heading: Document

16689.sourceSearchName: cloud service interoperability cloud service interoperability
16689.title: Cloud Service Interoperability
16689.heading: Cloud Service Interoperability
16689.content:
Cloud service interoperability is the capability to use the same or similar services across different cloud providers and to make cooperating services work together. Its scope includes data, processes, security, governance, monitoring, billing, reporting, and service management as well as technical protocols.

Interoperability enables provider substitution, federation, cloud bursting, and continuity. It requires common interfaces and compatible commitments rather than assuming that two services with similar marketing names can exchange work seamlessly.

16690.sourceSearchName: cloud service interoperability cloud service interoperability
16690.title: Cloud Service Interoperability
16690.heading: References

16691.sourceSearchName: cloud service integrator cloud service integrator
16691.title: Cloud Service Integrator
16691.heading: Document
16691.content:
2026-09-08 22:39

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Cloud Service Composition and Brokerage]]

16692.sourceSearchName: cloud service integrator cloud service integrator
16692.title: Cloud Service Integrator
16692.heading: Cloud Service Integrator
16692.content:
A cloud service integrator coordinates a portfolio of services so that it meets business needs consistently and efficiently. The role joins services across providers and connects those services to the organizational units that consume them.

The integrator may also consolidate contracts, reporting, and billing. Unlike a systems integrator focused on constructing a technical system, this role manages the continuing relationship and interoperability among delivered services.

16693.sourceSearchName: cloud service integrator cloud service integrator
16693.title: Cloud Service Integrator
16693.heading: References

16694.sourceSearchName: cloud service integration cloud service integration
16694.title: Cloud Service Integration
16694.heading: Document

16695.sourceSearchName: cloud service integration cloud service integration
16695.title: Cloud Service Integration
16695.heading: Cloud Service Integration
16695.content:
Cloud service integration coordinates several delivered services so that they form a consistent portfolio for a business. It connects providers with one another and connects their services to the organizational units that consume them.

Integration includes more than exchanging application data. Contracts, service levels, identity, monitoring, reports, and bills may also need common forms so the combined service can be operated and evaluated as a whole.

16696.sourceSearchName: cloud service integration cloud service integration
16696.title: Cloud Service Integration
16696.heading: References

16697.sourceSearchName: cloud service exchange cloud service exchange
16697.title: Cloud Service Exchange
16697.heading: Document
16697.content:
2026-09-08 22:39

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Cloud Service Composition and Brokerage]]

16698.sourceSearchName: cloud service exchange cloud service exchange
16698.title: Cloud Service Exchange
16698.heading: Cloud Service Exchange
16698.content:
A cloud service exchange is a proposed marketplace in which standardized cloud services could be discovered, priced, bought, and sold in real time. Supply and demand would help establish price, while service patterns would classify comparable offerings.

The idea depends on strong [[Cloud Service Interoperability]] so one provider's service can replace another without a long migration. Lower-level infrastructure and platform services are easier to commoditize this way than specialized business processes.

16699.sourceSearchName: cloud service exchange cloud service exchange
16699.title: Cloud Service Exchange
16699.heading: References

16700.sourceSearchName: cloud service creator cloud service creator
16700.title: Cloud Service Creator
16700.heading: Document
16700.content:
2026-09-08 22:39

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Cloud Service Composition and Brokerage]]

16701.sourceSearchName: cloud service creator cloud service creator
16701.title: Cloud Service Creator
16701.heading: Cloud Service Creator
16701.content:
A cloud service creator designs and builds a service that can be supplied through a [[Cloud Service Provider]]. Its work includes marshaling and optimizing the resources, components, interfaces, and management practices that underpin the offering.

The creator and provider may be the same entity, but separating the roles clarifies the supply chain. The creator produces a reusable capability; the provider contracts, orchestrates, and delivers that capability to a consumer.

16702.sourceSearchName: cloud service creator cloud service creator
16702.title: Cloud Service Creator
16702.heading: References

16703.sourceSearchName: cloud service consumer cloud service consumer
16703.title: Cloud Service Consumer
16703.heading: Document
16703.content:
2026-09-08 22:39

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Cloud Service Composition and Brokerage]]

16704.sourceSearchName: cloud service consumer cloud service consumer
16704.title: Cloud Service Consumer
16704.heading: Cloud Service Consumer
16704.content:
A cloud service consumer is the person or organization that uses a [[Cloud Service]]. The consumer evaluates candidates by the value they deliver, including cost, quality, timeliness, scope, security, and the ability to satisfy a real requirement.

A service catalog can record approved choices and their commitments. Before selecting a service, the consumer should compare its [[Service Level Agreement]], pricing basis, data obligations, continuity provisions, and dependency on its provider.

16705.sourceSearchName: cloud service consumer cloud service consumer
16705.title: Cloud Service Consumer
16705.heading: References

16706.sourceSearchName: cloud service encapsulation cloud service encapsulation
16706.title: Cloud Service Encapsulation
16706.heading: Document
16706.content:
2026-09-08 22:39

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Cloud Service Composition and Brokerage]]

16707.sourceSearchName: cloud service encapsulation cloud service encapsulation
16707.title: Cloud Service Encapsulation
16707.heading: Cloud Service Encapsulation
16707.content:
Cloud service encapsulation places one or more cloud services inside a larger service boundary. Consumers of the larger service can depend on what a component does without needing every detail of how that component is built.

The book distinguishes two forms: [[Cloud Service Aggregation]] for comparable repeated components and [[Cloud Service Composition]] for distinct cooperating components. Both can improve reuse and provisioning speed when their interfaces are standardized.

16708.sourceSearchName: cloud service encapsulation cloud service encapsulation
16708.title: Cloud Service Encapsulation
16708.heading: References

16709.sourceSearchName: cloud service continuity cloud service continuity
16709.title: Cloud Service Continuity
16709.heading: Document

16710.sourceSearchName: cloud service continuity cloud service continuity
16710.title: Cloud Service Continuity
16710.heading: Cloud Service Continuity
16710.content:
Cloud service continuity preserves a useful service when its primary provider or capacity becomes unavailable. A secondary service can support disaster recovery or accept overflow demand when the first service cannot satisfy its commitment.

Continuity across clouds requires compatible interfaces, data, processes, security, and control transfer. [[Cloud Bursting]] can automate part of the switch, but it must be exercised before a disruption to show that the secondary service is genuinely usable.

16711.sourceSearchName: cloud service continuity cloud service continuity
16711.title: Cloud Service Continuity
16711.heading: References

16712.sourceSearchName: cloud service composition cloud service composition
16712.title: Cloud Service Composition
16712.heading: Document
16712.content:
2026-09-08 22:39

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Cloud Service Composition and Brokerage]]

16713.sourceSearchName: cloud service composition cloud service composition
16713.title: Cloud Service Composition
16713.heading: Cloud Service Composition
16713.content:
Cloud service composition combines distinct cloud services or cells into a new service. Unlike [[Cloud Service Aggregation]], the components perform different functions that contribute to the whole.

Standardized interfaces, requirements, and management characteristics make components reusable across compositions. Changes to a standard cell must be tested in every composite service that uses its replicas because one update can affect several contexts.

16714.sourceSearchName: cloud service composition cloud service composition
16714.title: Cloud Service Composition
16714.heading: References

16715.sourceSearchName: cloud service commoditization cloud service commoditization
16715.title: Cloud Service Commoditization
16715.heading: Document

16716.sourceSearchName: cloud service commoditization cloud service commoditization
16716.title: Cloud Service Commoditization
16716.heading: Cloud Service Commoditization
16716.content:
Cloud service commoditization turns computing capabilities into standardized services that can be selected and purchased with less specialist knowledge. Reusable offerings, measurable units, common patterns, and provider competition make infrastructure and software resemble other utilities.

Standardization can lower cost and speed procurement, but it can also concentrate supply and hide meaningful differences. Interoperability and transparent service commitments are required before apparently comparable services can be substituted safely.

16717.sourceSearchName: cloud service commoditization cloud service commoditization
16717.title: Cloud Service Commoditization
16717.heading: References

16718.sourceSearchName: cloud service catalog cloud service catalog
16718.title: Cloud Service Catalog
16718.heading: Document
16718.content:
2026-09-08 22:39

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Cloud Service Composition and Brokerage]]

16719.sourceSearchName: cloud service catalog cloud service catalog
16719.title: Cloud Service Catalog
16719.heading: Cloud Service Catalog
16719.content:
A cloud service catalog is an organized list of services available to a defined group of consumers. Each entry can state what the service does, who supplies it, its price, its contract, and the service levels expected from it.

The catalog turns cloud procurement into a governed choice rather than an untracked individual purchase. A central IT function or [[Cloud Service Broker]] can maintain approved entries while allowing business users to select services suited to their needs.

16720.sourceSearchName: cloud service catalog cloud service catalog
16720.title: Cloud Service Catalog
16720.heading: References

16721.sourceSearchName: cloud queue message cloud queue message
16721.title: Cloud Queue Message
16721.heading: Document
16721.content:
2026-09-08 22:09

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Azure Blob and Queue Storage]]

16722.sourceSearchName: cloud queue message cloud queue message
16722.title: Cloud Queue Message
16722.heading: Cloud Queue Message
16722.content:
A cloud queue message is the discrete payload placed on an Azure Storage Queue. The order generator serializes a sales-order object into the message, and the worker reverses that representation after retrieving it.

A message should carry the information required to process its work without forcing a direct dependency on the producer. Size, ordering, retry, deletion, and duplicate-handling assumptions belong to the message contract.

16723.sourceSearchName: cloud queue message cloud queue message
16723.title: Cloud Queue Message
16723.heading: References

16724.sourceSearchName: cloud service broker cloud service broker
16724.title: Cloud Service Broker
16724.heading: Document
16724.content:
2026-09-08 22:39

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Cloud Service Composition and Brokerage]]

16725.sourceSearchName: cloud service broker cloud service broker
16725.title: Cloud Service Broker
16725.heading: Cloud Service Broker
16725.content:
A cloud service broker is an intermediary between consumers and one or more cloud service providers. It can reduce provider lock-in, aggregate several services into one offering, and choose or orchestrate providers according to cost, quality, and timeliness.

The broker negotiates upstream prices and [[Service Level Agreement|service agreements]], then presents a consolidated relationship to the consumer. A broker may maintain a [[Cloud Service Catalog]] and perform integration so the consumer does not have to coordinate every supplier separately.

16726.sourceSearchName: cloud service broker cloud service broker
16726.title: Cloud Service Broker
16726.heading: References

16727.sourceSearchName: cloud service aggregation cloud service aggregation
16727.title: Cloud Service Aggregation
16727.heading: Document
16727.content:
2026-09-08 22:39

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Cloud Service Composition and Brokerage]]

16728.sourceSearchName: cloud service aggregation cloud service aggregation
16728.title: Cloud Service Aggregation
16728.heading: Cloud Service Aggregation
16728.content:
Cloud service aggregation combines comparable cloud cells or services into a larger service. Replicas can share demand, operate from different data centers, or be supplied by different providers while presenting one capability to the consumer.

Aggregation supports elasticity, cloud bursting, continuity, and reuse. Because the components are intended to fulfill the same role, their interfaces and service commitments need to be compatible enough for work to move between them.

16729.sourceSearchName: cloud service aggregation cloud service aggregation
16729.title: Cloud Service Aggregation
16729.heading: References

16730.sourceSearchName: cloud profit margin cloud profit margin
16730.title: Cloud Profit Margin
16730.heading: Document
16730.content:
2026-09-08 22:39

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Cloud Business Value and Finance]]

16731.sourceSearchName: cloud profit margin cloud profit margin
16731.title: Cloud Profit Margin
16731.heading: Cloud Profit Margin
16731.content:
Cloud profit margin is the portion of business value left after the costs of delivering a cloud-supported product or service. Shared provider scale, reusable services, and lower up-front infrastructure can move the break-even point and reduce some delivery costs.

The margin is not guaranteed by adopting cloud technology. Service price, integration work, support, risk, demand, and the revenue actually enabled must all be included when comparing cloud delivery with an owned environment.

16732.sourceSearchName: cloud profit margin cloud profit margin
16732.title: Cloud Profit Margin
16732.heading: References

16733.sourceSearchName: cloud price model cloud price model
16733.title: Cloud Price Model
16733.heading: Document

16734.sourceSearchName: cloud price model cloud price model
16734.title: Cloud Price Model
16734.heading: Cloud Price Model
16734.content:
A cloud price model defines the rule used to calculate what a consumer pays for a cloud service. It is derived from the provider's cost model but also reflects business strategy, expected revenue, transferred risk, market positioning, and the value unit visible to the customer.

Pricing can follow resource use, transactions, subscriptions, volume, service commitments, outcomes, or marketing strategy. A useful comparison normalizes the unit and term rather than comparing only the headline monthly amounts.

16735.sourceSearchName: cloud price model cloud price model
16735.title: Cloud Price Model
16735.heading: References

16736.sourceSearchName: cloud price flexibility cloud price flexibility
16736.title: Cloud Price Flexibility
16736.heading: Document
16736.content:
2026-09-08 22:39

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Cloud Business Value and Finance]]

16737.sourceSearchName: cloud price flexibility cloud price flexibility
16737.title: Cloud Price Flexibility
16737.heading: Cloud Price Flexibility
16737.content:
Cloud price flexibility is the ability to change pricing arrangements as demand, volume, and circumstances evolve. A consumption model may suit a small or irregular workload, while a volume, tiered, or performance model may become more valuable as use grows.

The consumer can seek a different plan from the same provider or move to another provider when interoperability permits. The value comes from avoiding a permanently fixed cost structure that no longer matches the workload.

16738.sourceSearchName: cloud price flexibility cloud price flexibility
16738.title: Cloud Price Flexibility
16738.heading: References

16739.sourceSearchName: cloud payroll service cloud payroll service
16739.title: Cloud Payroll Service
16739.heading: Document

16740.sourceSearchName: cloud payroll service cloud payroll service
16740.title: Cloud Payroll Service
16740.heading: Cloud Payroll Service
16740.content:
A cloud payroll service delivers salary calculation, payment, payslip processing, and required tax transfer as a repeatable hosted process. Its per-record workload and common use across industries make it a horizontal business-process service.

The process depends on interfaces to human resources and management for events such as unpaid leave, overtime, and departure dates. Standard delivery improves consistency only when those inputs remain accurate and timely.

16741.sourceSearchName: cloud payroll service cloud payroll service
16741.title: Cloud Payroll Service
16741.heading: References

16743.title: Cloud of Things and Services
16743.heading: Cloud of Things and Services
16743.content:
A cloud of things and services combines connected devices with the cloud-hosted workflows that monitor and support them. The book uses this term for a specialist cloud joining the Internet of Things with the [[Internet of Services]].

Automation is its central premise: sensed conditions can trigger maintenance, information, billing, or control at the place where a device is located. The cloud can use public, private, community, or hybrid deployment according to the devices and consumers involved.

16745.title: Cloud of Things

16746.sourceSearchName: cloud of things cloud of things
16746.title: Cloud of Things
16746.heading: Cloud of Things
16746.content:
A cloud of things is a cloud service whose scope is the management or use of connected nonliving objects. Sensors report state or location, and cloud-hosted logic can monitor, coordinate, or control devices for people and organizations.

Examples include lighting, appliances, buildings, vehicles, and health-monitoring equipment. Device identity, network reach, automation, data ownership, location, and service availability become part of the system rather than properties of the physical object alone.

16747.sourceSearchName: cloud of things cloud of things
16747.title: Cloud of Things
16747.heading: References

16749.title: Cloud Monitoring and Alerting
16749.heading: Cloud Monitoring and Alerting
16749.content:
Cloud monitoring and alerting observe service health, use, capacity, and failures and notify responsible people or automated processes when action is needed. Interoperating services benefit from common alert formats and routes so one team can interpret them consistently.

Proactive stress and security tests can supplement operational signals. Monitoring supports remediation only when thresholds relate to service requirements and alerts lead to owned, timely response procedures.

16752.title: Cloud Health Monitoring Service
16752.heading: Cloud Health Monitoring Service
16752.content:
A cloud health monitoring service collects measurements from personal or wearable devices, analyzes them, and alerts an individual or nominated caregiver when defined conditions occur. The workflow joins sensing, transmission, storage, analysis, and notification.

Aggregated anonymized measurements can also support population-level analysis, while individual data remains subject to strong privacy and consent boundaries. A prediction or threshold alert supports attention; it does not replace clinical judgment.

16755.sourceSearchName: cloud maturity model cloud maturity model
16755.title: Cloud Maturity Model
16755.heading: Cloud Maturity Model
16755.content:
A cloud maturity model assesses how deliberately an organization purchases, uses, controls, and improves cloud services. The book defines five stages: performed, defined, managed, adapted, and optimized.

Maturity can be assessed separately for people, processes, monitoring and reporting, oversight, and financial management. The overall level reflects where most characteristics coincide, while differences among dimensions identify the next practical improvements.

16758.title: Cloud Gear
16758.heading: Cloud Gear
16758.content:
A cloud gear is a specialist form of [[Cloud Cell]] used mainly in infrastructure or platform services. It packages a focused supporting application such as antivirus protection, disk encryption, public file sharing, or backup.

Treating the capability as a reusable unit allows it to be attached to more than one cloud service instead of being rebuilt for every environment. Its interface and management requirements must be standardized for that reuse to be dependable.

16761.title: Cloud Governance
16761.heading: Cloud Governance
16761.content:
Cloud governance is the organizational oversight used to keep cloud services aligned with business needs, standards, security policy, regulation, and financial constraints. It defines who may choose services, which controls apply, and how performance and risk are reviewed.

Interoperating services should remain under compatible governance rather than falling between separate owners. A governance board, catalog, audit process, and reporting practices convert policy into recurring decisions and evidence.

16764.heading: Cloud Cost-Benefit Analysis
16764.content:
A cloud cost-benefit analysis compares the full costs of a cloud service with the benefits it is expected to deliver. Benefits can include flexible capacity, earlier revenue, broader access, lower asset ownership, and more attention available for the organization's primary work.

The analysis should use comparable time periods and include switching, integration, support, risk, and dependency rather than only the advertised subscription. [[Net Present Value]], [[Return on Investment]], and [[Payback Period]] turn parts of the comparison into financial measures.

16767.heading: Cloud Examination Service
16767.content:
A cloud examination service delivers identity checking, authorization, question selection, supervision, scoring, and result handling as an integrated process. A large question bank can vary test instances while keeping the assessment rules consistent.

Remote delivery requires credible evidence that the authorized person completed the examination under the intended conditions. The process should integrate with training rather than treating assessment as an unrelated final event.

16770.title: Cloud Federation
16770.heading: Cloud Federation
16770.content:
Cloud federation is a composition of services supplied by disparate clouds, commonly across provider boundaries. The resulting service can mix an organization's own cloud cells with third-party cells or can be assembled entirely from external providers.

Federation can add capacity, augment a service rapidly, balance work, or provide failure safety. It relies on [[Cloud Service Interoperability]] because the components must exchange data and control despite being owned and operated separately.

16773.heading: Cloud Deployment Model
16773.content:
A cloud deployment model describes the scope of the community allowed to consume a cloud and the network or ownership boundary around it. It is independent of the [[Cloud Service Model]] that describes what level of capability is delivered.

The four models are [[Public Cloud]], [[Private Cloud]], [[Community Cloud]], and [[Hybrid Cloud]]. Any service abstraction can be offered through a suitable deployment model, so a service should be described by both dimensions when the distinction matters.

16776.title: Cloud Demand Flexibility
16776.heading: Cloud Demand Flexibility
16776.content:
Cloud demand flexibility is the ability to change computing capacity as a product or service moves through development, testing, launch, promotion, ordinary use, and decline. Each stage can create a different peak or trough in demand.

[[Rapid Elasticity]] lets spending and capacity follow those changes rather than requiring permanent overprovisioning. The value appears as both avoided idle investment and a lower chance of losing business during unexpected peaks.

A cloud data science platform supplies remotely accessible computation, storage, and analytic software. It can place a consistent environment near shared data and reduce the need to configure every analyst's machine independently.

Remote access does not remove governance or reproducibility requirements; data access, versions, and execution environments still need to be recorded.

16782.content:
A cloud critical success factor is a condition that must be satisfied for an adopted service to deliver its intended value. It converts an important requirement into a focus for design, measurement, ownership, and review.

Success factors can concern interoperability, resilience, security, support, financial viability, or process readiness. They should be specific enough to guide a decision and be tested throughout adoption rather than declared only after deployment.

16785.title: Cloud Cost Model
16785.heading: Cloud Cost Model
16785.content:
A cloud cost model estimates what a provider must spend to create, operate, maintain, and eventually refresh a cloud service. It can include equipment, capital, labor, software licenses, electricity, cooling, floor space, depreciation, inflation, and exchange-rate effects.

Risk and a desired margin are added to those costs before they become a [[Cloud Price Model]]. One-time costs can be converted into recurring amounts so the provider can express the service as a regular charge.

16787.title: Cloud Computing Model
16787.heading: Document

16788.sourceSearchName: cloud computing model cloud computing model
16788.title: Cloud Computing Model
16788.heading: Cloud Computing Model
16788.content:
Cloud computing provides on-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources that can be provisioned and released with little direct management effort. The resources can include networks, servers, storage, applications, and complete services.

The model combines [[Broad Network Access]], [[On-Demand Self-Service]], [[Resource Pooling]], [[Rapid Elasticity]], and [[Measured Cloud Service|measured use]]. [[Server Virtualization]] can help implement these properties, but virtualization alone is not cloud computing because it does not necessarily include automated provisioning, service measurement, reporting, or billing.

16789.sourceSearchName: cloud computing model cloud computing model
16789.title: Cloud Computing Model
16789.heading: References

16791.title: Cloud Compliance
16791.heading: Cloud Compliance
16791.content:
Cloud compliance is adherence to the laws, industry regulations, policies, and contractual standards that apply to a cloud service and its data. General services may face broad rules, while specialist services can inherit additional industry and local requirements.

Every interoperating component within a regulated process must meet the applicable obligations. Provider location, hosting location, users, data subjects, and service purpose can all affect the compliance scope.

16793.title: Cloud Cell

16794.title: Cloud Cell
16794.heading: Cloud Cell
16794.content:
A cloud cell is a cloud unit that provides one distinct, fundamental function which other clouds can reuse. Examples include a database cell, storage cell, web-server cell, service-bus cell, or firewall cell.

The cell exposes an interface and can be combined through [[Cloud Service Aggregation]], [[Cloud Service Composition]], or [[Cloud Federation]]. Standard definitions and management characteristics make replicas easier to provision and maintain across several composite services.

16796.title: Cloud Bursting

16797.title: Cloud Bursting
16797.heading: Cloud Bursting
16797.content:
Cloud bursting moves excess work from one cloud to capacity supplied by another when the first cloud cannot meet demand. It extends elasticity across a cloud or provider boundary rather than only adding resources inside one pool.

The secondary service must be compatible enough to accept the work, data, and control state. Contracts, security, performance, and [[Cloud Service Interoperability]] therefore determine whether bursting can occur automatically without breaking the original service commitment.

16799.sourceSearchName: cloud billing and reporting cloud billing and reporting
16799.title: Cloud Billing and Reporting
16799.heading: Document

16800.sourceSearchName: cloud billing and reporting cloud billing and reporting
16800.title: Cloud Billing and Reporting
16800.heading: Cloud Billing and Reporting
16800.content:
Cloud billing and reporting translate measured service use into statements that consumers can understand and reconcile with contracts. Reports should connect price units, usage, service performance, and time periods rather than presenting an unexplained total.

Common processes and formats make costs from several providers easier to consolidate and compare. Frequent reporting also lets consumers detect unexpected demand or a misconfigured service before the cost grows unnoticed.

16803.sourceSearchName: cloud backup service cloud backup service
16803.title: Cloud Backup Service
16803.heading: Cloud Backup Service
16803.content:
A cloud backup service receives and retains recovery copies over a network. It can provide remote location, elastic storage, monitoring, and recurring schedules without requiring the consumer to operate a separate physical backup server.

The service does not remove backup design. The consumer must define the fileset, scheme, retention, encryption, provider independence, bandwidth, and restoration objectives before the remote copy becomes dependable recovery capability.

16805.sourceSearchName: cloud automation and productivity cloud automation and productivity
16805.title: Cloud Automation and Productivity
16805.heading: Document

16806.sourceSearchName: cloud automation and productivity cloud automation and productivity
16806.title: Cloud Automation and Productivity
16806.heading: Cloud Automation and Productivity
16806.content:
Cloud automation and productivity describes the value created when readily available computing services let organizations automate work without first building a full infrastructure estate. Applications, information, and workflows can be provisioned as recurring operating services.

Automation can remove manual delay and let people concentrate on the organization's main work. It can also displace existing tasks and create dependency on remote services, so productivity gains should be evaluated alongside workforce, continuity, and control effects.

16807.sourceSearchName: cloud automation and productivity cloud automation and productivity
16807.title: Cloud Automation and Productivity
16807.heading: References

16809.title: Cloud Auditing
16809.heading: Cloud Auditing
16809.content:
Cloud auditing examines whether a cloud service and its use conform to agreed policies, contracts, standards, and controls. It relies on evidence such as configurations, access records, service reports, bills, test results, and remediation history.

When several services interoperate, they should be subject to compatible audit expectations and common oversight. A gap at one provider can undermine the combined process even if every other component is reviewed carefully.

16812.heading: Cloud Asset Optimization
16812.content:
Cloud asset optimization reduces the need to own computing capacity sized for a workload's highest anticipated demand. Permanently overprovisioned equipment consumes capital, space, power, and maintenance even when business activity is low.

Elastic services can supply capacity during peaks and release it as a product declines. The organization then avoids being left with obsolete or unnecessary infrastructure whose life cycle no longer matches the product it supports.

16815.heading: Cloud Application Development Platform

A cloud application development platform supplies a standardized runtime, tools, libraries, and supporting services so developers can build and deploy without first procuring the infrastructure stack. Ready-made storage and database services can become application building blocks.

The model can shorten the develop-build-test-deploy cycle and let capacity grow with an application's users. The convenience may create [[Vendor Lock-In]] when code, data, or operational procedures depend strongly on provider-specific facilities.

A cloud application testing environment is a temporary or reusable platform provisioned to validate software without permanently owning its peak infrastructure. It can expand for load, stress, performance, security, integration, system, or acceptance tests and contract after the test finishes.

The strategy should be driven by requirements and business processes rather than by the availability of a technology. Provider selection, security, interoperability, continuity, pricing, governance, and organizational responsibility all influence the transition path.

A cloud abstraction level indicates how much of the underlying technology a service consumer must specify or manage. At a low level, the consumer chooses infrastructure details; at a high level, the consumer asks for information or a completed business outcome.

Increasing abstraction can reduce technical management and let the consumer focus on purpose. It also transfers more control and dependency to the provider, making interfaces, service commitments, data access, and portability more important.

16829.sourceSearchName: closure theorem for elimination closure theorem for elimination
16829.title: Closure Theorem for Elimination
16829.heading: Document

16830.sourceSearchName: closure theorem for elimination closure theorem for elimination
16830.title: Closure Theorem for Elimination
16830.heading: Closure Theorem for Elimination
16830.content:
The closure theorem states that the variety of an elimination ideal is the smallest [[Affine Variety]] containing the projection of the original variety. It is therefore the [[Zariski Closure]] of that projected image.

When the original variety is nonempty, points outside a smaller exceptional subvariety can be lifted back to the original solution set. The theorem connects symbolic variable elimination with geometric projection.

16831.sourceSearchName: closure theorem for elimination closure theorem for elimination
16831.title: Closure Theorem for Elimination
16831.heading: References

16833.title: Closure Property
16833.heading: Closure Property
16833.content:
A collection is closed under an operation when applying that operation to any allowed inputs always produces another member of the same collection. For natural numbers (a) and (b), both (a+b) and (ab) are natural numbers, so (mathbb{N}) is closed under addition and multiplication.

Closure depends on both the operation and the number system. Natural numbers are not closed under subtraction or division, because results such as (3-5) and (3/5) leave the set. [[Integer]]s repair closure under subtraction, while [[Rational Number]]s also accommodate division by nonzero values.

16835.sourceSearchName: closest cluster pair selection closest cluster pair selection
16835.title: Closest Cluster Pair Selection
16835.heading: Document

16836.sourceSearchName: closest cluster pair selection closest cluster pair selection
16836.title: Closest Cluster Pair Selection
16836.heading: Closest Cluster Pair Selection
16836.content:
At each agglomerative step, the linkage routine finds the smallest stored distance among currently unmerged clusters. It removes the chosen pair from active state and uses their distance as the join value of a new parent.

A straightforward scan is simple but can dominate runtime as the matrix grows. Whatever selection structure is used must ignore obsolete pairs after clusters are merged.

16837.sourceSearchName: closest cluster pair selection closest cluster pair selection
16837.title: Closest Cluster Pair Selection
16837.heading: References

16838.sourceSearchName: closed nested transaction closed nested transaction
16838.title: Closed Nested Transaction
16838.heading: Document

16839.sourceSearchName: closed nested transaction closed nested transaction
16839.title: Closed Nested Transaction
16839.heading: Closed Nested Transaction
16839.content:
A closed nested transaction may commit internally, but its effects remain part of the parent's tentative state and are not independently visible outside the nesting hierarchy. If the parent aborts, the inner effects are rolled back with it.

Closed nesting preserves strong isolation while allowing an inner failure to be retried without restarting unrelated inner work.

16840.title: Closed Nested Transaction
16840.heading: References

16842.sourceSearchName: closed cycle mhd system closed cycle mhd system
16842.title: Closed-Cycle MHD System
16842.heading: Closed-Cycle MHD System
16842.content: A closed-cycle MHD system reheats and recirculates its working fluid instead of exhausting combustion gas after one duct passage. The source describes argon or helium heated through a heat exchanger, then seeded to conduct or mixed with conductive liquid metal. After electrical extraction, the fluid is slowed, cooled, compressed, and reheated. This separates combustion products from the generator flow but adds loop equipment.

16843.sourceSearchName: closed cycle mhd system closed cycle mhd system
16843.title: Closed-Cycle MHD System
16843.heading: References

16845.title: Closed Endpoint
16845.heading: Closed Endpoint
16845.content:
A closed endpoint is a boundary value included in an [[Interval]]. It corresponds to an inclusive inequality such as (x\leq2) or (x\geq-1).

On a [[Number Line]], inclusion is shown with a filled point at the boundary. In interval notation, a bracket is used for a finite endpoint. The equality portion of (\leq) or (\geq) is what admits the boundary. A strict comparison instead produces an [[Open Endpoint]].

16847.sourceSearchName: closed sequential pattern closed sequential pattern
16847.title: Closed Sequential Pattern
16847.heading: Document

16848.sourceSearchName: closed sequential pattern closed sequential pattern
16848.title: Closed Sequential Pattern
16848.heading: Closed Sequential Pattern
16848.content:
A closed sequential pattern is a frequent sequence pattern for which no strictly more specific superpattern has the same support. Retaining closed patterns removes support-equivalent redundancy without losing the frequency information of the full frequent set.

Closedness compresses the candidate space before feature mapping. It does not guarantee predictive usefulness, so class discrimination or downstream selection may still be needed.

16849.sourceSearchName: closed sequential pattern closed sequential pattern
16849.title: Closed Sequential Pattern
16849.heading: References

16850.sourceSearchName: clone match verification clone match verification
16850.title: Clone Match Verification
16850.heading: Document

16851.sourceSearchName: clone match verification clone match verification
16851.title: Clone Match Verification
16851.heading: Clone Match Verification
16851.content:
Clone match verification tests whether feature correspondences actually support a duplicated image region. Candidate pairs should agree under a shared transformation, form a spatially meaningful cluster, and yield strong correlation between the transformed source pixels and proposed copy.

This stage rejects accidental descriptor matches and legitimate repeated objects. Blending, compression, and partial occlusion can lower correlation, so verification balances tolerance for post-processing against the risk of accepting ordinary repetition as tampering.

16852.sourceSearchName: clone match verification clone match verification
16852.title: Clone Match Verification
16852.heading: References

16854.title: Clone Detection
16854.heading: Clone Detection
16854.content:
Clone detection finds duplicated regions that may indicate a [[Copy-Move Image Forgery]]. Exhaustively comparing every possible patch is computationally impractical, so a detector first identifies distinctive locations, represents their neighborhoods compactly, and retrieves similar candidates.

Candidate pairs are grouped by a consistent translation, rotation, or scale and then checked against the underlying pixels. Verification is crucial because windows, bricks, foliage, and other repeated scene structures can generate legitimate matches.

16856.sourceSearchName: clocked cpu cycle clocked cpu cycle
16856.title: Clocked CPU Cycle
16856.heading: Document

16857.sourceSearchName: clocked cpu cycle clocked cpu cycle
16857.title: Clocked CPU Cycle
16857.heading: Clocked CPU Cycle
16857.content:
A clocked CPU uses regular timing pulses to separate one computational step from the next. Each interval allows signals to propagate through logic circuits and settle before their outputs are captured in registers.

The clock turns an abstract sequence of algorithmic steps into coordinated physical events. If the interval is too short, unstable signals may be recorded and corrupt later operations.

16858.sourceSearchName: clocked cpu cycle clocked cpu cycle
16858.title: Clocked CPU Cycle
16858.heading: References

16860.title: CLIQUE Monotonicity
16860.heading: CLIQUE Monotonicity
16860.content:
CLIQUE monotonicity states that if a unit is dense in a set of dimensions, every projection of that unit onto fewer dimensions is also dense under the corresponding support threshold. An infrequent lower-dimensional unit therefore eliminates all of its higher-dimensional extensions.

This property supports an Apriori-like levelwise search through subspaces. It reduces computation but does not eliminate redundant descriptions when the same objects form dense units in many related projections.

16866.title: CLIQUE Grid Subspace Clustering
16866.heading: CLIQUE Grid Subspace Clustering
16866.content:
CLIQUE divides each dimension into intervals, identifies dense units, and joins adjacent dense units into clusters within subspaces. It uses the fact that a dense unit in a high-dimensional subspace must also be dense in every lower-dimensional projection.

This downward-closure property prunes much of the subspace search. The resulting descriptions are interpretable as unions of grid units, although density and interval parameters can produce fragmented or redundant clusters.

16869.content: Climb charts relate pressure altitude and temperature to climb speed, rate, time, distance, and fuel required. Weight and starting altitude remain essential assumptions when applying those relationships in [[Climb, Cruise, and Leg Fuel Planning]].

16872.title: Client-Side Validation
16872.heading: Client-Side Validation
16872.content:
Client-side validation checks form values in the browser and provides immediate feedback before a request is submitted. Required fields, lengths, numeric ranges, and pattern rules can be reflected directly in the form model and template.

This improves user experience but is not a security boundary. A caller can bypass the Angular interface, so every important rule must also be enforced through [[Server-Side Validation]].

16875.sourceSearchName: client side paging client side paging
16875.title: Client-Side Paging
16875.heading: Client-Side Paging
16875.content:
Client-side paging fetches a complete result set and divides it into pages inside the browser. Page changes are fast after the initial response because they do not require another server request.

The approach becomes inefficient when the dataset is large: the server still queries and transfers every row, and the client stores and processes values the user may never view. [[Server-Side Paging]] avoids that cost by requesting one slice at a time.

16878.content:
Client-side debugging observes JavaScript or TypeScript behavior running in the browser. It can inspect component variables, form controls, subscriptions, network requests, and changes to the rendered document.

A [[JavaScript Source Map]] allows a debugger to connect generated JavaScript back to the original TypeScript. Browser developer tools provide an additional view of console messages, source files, requests, and element state.

16881.title: Client-Side Blazor
16881.heading: Client-Side Blazor
16881.content:
Client-side Blazor is the 2019 preview model in which the browser downloads a .NET runtime and application assemblies and executes C# locally through WebAssembly. Interface events can update the page without a server call after the application is loaded.

Local execution enables a C# client but adds an initial download that affects startup. The source explicitly treats this hosting model as not yet part of the official .NET Core 3 release, so its statements describe that historical preview.

16884.title: Client-Server Game Topology
16884.heading: Client-Server Game Topology
16884.content:
A client-server game topology gives a server authoritative responsibility for shared game state while clients send input and receive results. Central authority simplifies validation and resolves disagreements among participants.

A dedicated server runs separately from players, while a listen server also hosts a local player. Server capacity, latency, and failure become central constraints, but clients need not trust one another's claims directly.

16887.heading: Client-Server Evolution from Time-Sharing
16887.content:
Client-server computing distributes work between user-controlled machines and powerful shared servers. Servers manage large datasets and common services, while clients handle interaction, graphics, and some computation.

The arrangement evolved from time-sharing but replaced passive terminals with capable networked computers. It preserves shared resources without surrendering responsive local control.

16890.sourceSearchName: client endpoint security client endpoint security
16890.title: Client Endpoint Security
16890.heading: Client Endpoint Security
16890.content:
Client endpoint security protects the device from which a person reaches a cloud service. Malware, stolen credentials, unsafe applications, or a compromised browser can defeat server-side controls by impersonating an otherwise legitimate user.

Anti-malware, local firewalls, careful credential handling, timely updates, and restricted data storage reduce this risk. Thin or centrally managed clients can narrow the endpoint's responsibilities, but user behavior and device access remain part of the end-to-end security boundary.

16893.sourceSearchName: client cache aside pattern client cache aside pattern
16893.title: Client Cache-Aside Pattern
16893.heading: Client Cache-Aside Pattern
16893.content:
Client cache-aside makes the mobile application check a local cache before requesting an entity from a remote service. A cache miss triggers the network request and stores the returned value for later reads.

The pattern can keep screens responsive and permit limited offline use, but application code owns freshness and invalidation. A cached result should be presented with an explicit understanding of when it was obtained and how it will be reconciled with server data.

16896.title: CLICK Clustering
16896.heading: CLICK Clustering
16896.content:
CLICK, Clique Clustering using K-partite graphs, represents categorical attribute values as parts of a graph and connects strongly related values across attributes. It detects maximal multipartite cliques as candidate clusters.

Preprocessing builds the graph and clique matrix, detection finds strongly connected cliques, and postprocessing validates and merges supported candidates.
